Chapter 9. The Role of Imagination and the Courage to Dream
Picture this—it's the end of a long meeting. The room is almost empty, chairs are pushed back, and the coffee sitting on the table has lost its warmth. Out of nowhere, someone asks a question that hangs in the air, almost like a secret: “What would it look like if we actually won?”
At first, there's just silence. Most folks are so used to working with whatever scraps they can get, so the idea of true victory almost feels too bold to say out loud. But then, little by little, the conversation picks up.
Someone shares a vision of a city where having a safe home isn’t just for the lucky ones—it’s a right for everyone. Another person starts to imagine schools where every single kid is welcomed, no barriers at all. Someone else dreams up a workplace where decisions aren’t just handed down from above, but made together, as a team.
Suddenly, the room isn’t so empty anymore—it’s packed with possibility.
Most of us don’t realize just how powerful our imagination can be. It’s easy to believe that the way things are is the only way they could ever be. But here’s something important: every single movement for justice started with someone brave enough to dream of something better. Imagination isn’t just an escape from the struggle—it’s the fuel that keeps it going.
If you’ve spent years fighting for those tiny bits of progress, dreaming big might feel risky. It opens you up to disappointment, to being laughed at, to worrying you might fall short. But it also gives you back the future. It’s a way of saying, “No, things don’t have to stay this way.”
When the meeting wraps up, people head out with something new in their hearts—a sense of purpose that wasn’t there before. Sure, the path ahead is still tough and the challenges are real. But now, the dream is alive. And that changes everything.
Because the courage to imagine a better world? That’s the very first step to making it real.
